lessons.title: Phase-by-Phase Anatomy: Expansion, Peak, Contraction, Trough

body.text: Each phase of the cycle has a recognisable signature across indicators, policy, and markets. Learning that signature matters more than being able to name the phase precisely.

children.text: This lesson closes out Chapter 1 by pulling together everything so far: the phases from Lesson 1.1, the indicator categories from Lesson 1.2, and the caveats from Lesson 1.3, into a single working picture of what each phase actually looks like across data, RBI policy, and equity markets. Chapters 2 through 5 will each zoom into one piece of this picture in far more depth.

Growth is accelerating or holding at a high, broad-based pace. PMI sits comfortably above 55, credit growth is accelerating as banks extend more working capital and project finance, and the yield curve is typically normal to steep, since markets expect stronger growth and eventually higher rates ahead. Equity markets tend to rally broadly, with cyclicals, financials, and small and midcaps often outperforming as earnings upgrades outnumber downgrades across a wide set of sectors, not just a handful of large names.

Growth is still high but decelerating at the margin, and this is usually the hardest phase to call in real time, because the coincident and lagging data can still look excellent even as leading indicators start rolling over. PMI stays expansionary but growth in new orders slows, credit growth plateaus, and the yield curve begins flattening as the RBI moves into active tightening, often its fastest pace of hikes in the cycle, since inflation risk typically dominates the policy conversation here. In equities, index levels can remain near highs while market breadth quietly narrows: fewer stocks are actually participating in new highs, and quality, largecap names tend to start outperforming smaller, more cyclically geared ones.

As covered in Lesson 1.3, this is a sharp growth deceleration in India far more often than an outright contraction. PMI new orders fall toward or below the 50 line, credit growth decelerates sharply as banks turn cautious, and credit spreads widen visibly as default risk gets repriced. The RBI typically pauses first, then pivots toward cuts as growth risk starts to dominate inflation risk in its own reaction function. Equity markets broadly derate through this phase: small and midcaps usually underperform the most, an earnings downgrade cycle sets in across cyclical sectors, and traditionally defensive sectors such as FMCG, pharma, and utilities tend to hold up relatively better.

This is the phase Chapter 4 is built around, and the one with the widest gap between what leading and lagging data are saying. Leading indicators, credit growth momentum, PMI new orders, the yield curve, tend to stabilise and turn up first, while GDP growth and reported earnings, both lagging, are often still weak or only just beginning to turn. The RBI is usually already easing or holding at the bottom of its cycle by this point. This is also, historically, the phase where equity markets themselves move first: Indian markets have a track record of bottoming and beginning to recover before the growth data confirms the trough, which is exactly why this is the hardest phase to act on with confidence, and the most costly one to wait out.

body.text: Markets themselves behave as a leading indicator, not just a mirror of one. The Nifty bottomed around March 2009 and again around March 2020, both times well before GDP growth or reported earnings data confirmed the respective troughs. Waiting for confirmed lagging data before repositioning has historically meant missing a meaningful part of the subsequent recovery.

body.title: One Full Cycle, Labelled: FY19 to FY23

events.title: Peak Rolling Into Deceleration
events.description: Growth was already decelerating from over 7% toward around 4%, with an NBFC credit crunch visibly tightening credit growth well before Covid arrived.

events.title: Sharp Contraction
events.description: A global pandemic shock landed on top of an already-decelerating domestic cycle. GDP contracted outright, and the RBI cut the repo rate to a then record low alongside emergency liquidity measures.

events.title: Trough and Early Recovery
events.description: Leading indicators, PMI and credit growth among them, began turning up while GDP was still recovering off a depressed base. The Nifty had already bottomed in March 2020, months before growth data confirmed the trough.

events.title: Expansion Resumes, Then Peaks Again
events.description: Broad-based growth recovery took hold, before the RBI began a fresh hiking cycle from May 2022 as inflation picked up, the cycle's next transition from expansion toward peak.

body.title: Phase Recognition Checklist
steps: Check whether PMI new orders and the headline PMI print still agree in direction, or whether new orders, the more leading of the two, has started diverging
Check the direction of the RBI's last two policy moves, not just where the repo rate currently sits
Check whether corporate bond credit spreads over G-Secs are widening or narrowing from recent extremes
Check market breadth: is a rally or a decline broad-based across sectors and market caps, or is it concentrated in a handful of names
Use reported GDP growth and earnings only to confirm a read you already formed from leading and coincident data, not as your primary timing signal

body.title: Weigh the Signals
body.scenario: On the same day, you observe: the spread between the 10-year and 3-month G-Sec yield has compressed to near zero from about 150 basis points a year earlier, corporate bond spreads over G-Secs have widened by roughly 40 basis points over the last two quarters, the Nifty is down about 15% from its all-time high, but headline PMI Manufacturing is still at 54 and the latest reported quarterly GDP growth came in at 7.1%.
body.prompt: Which phase does this combination most resemble, and which signals should you weight most heavily in that judgement?
body.modelAnswer: This looks like Peak transitioning into Contraction/Deceleration, not continued Expansion. The yield curve compressing sharply, credit spreads widening, and the equity market correcting are all leading signals, and all three are pointing the same direction: toward a turn. PMI at 54 and GDP growth at 7.1% look reassuring, but both are coincident-to-lagging by the classification from Lesson 1.2, meaning they reflect where the economy already was, not where it is headed. The right approach, per this lesson's framework, is to weight the leading signals (curve, spreads, equity breadth and price action) more heavily than the still-strong lagging data, and treat the still-solid PMI and GDP prints as confirmation of the expansion that is ending, not evidence that a turn is not underway.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Based on India's history around 2009 and 2020, which statement about equity markets and the business cycle is most accurate?
options: Equity markets typically bottom only after GDP growth data confirms the trough
Equity markets have historically bottomed and begun recovering before growth data confirmed a trough, effectively acting as a leading indicator themselves
Equity markets and GDP growth always bottom in the exact same quarter
Equity market behaviour has no consistent relationship with the business cycle
body.explanation: The Nifty bottomed around March 2009 and again around March 2020, in both cases before GDP growth or reported earnings confirmed the trough had arrived. This is consistent with markets pricing in forward expectations, the same reason yield curves and credit spreads are classified as leading indicators in Lesson 1.2.

body.text: This lesson presents a general, educational framework for reading phase signatures. Typical phase durations and the FY19-FY23 timeline are simplified for teaching purposes; actual cycles vary, and none of this constitutes investment advice or a specific market call.

points: Each phase has a recognisable signature across leading indicators, RBI policy stance, and equity market behaviour, not just a growth rate range
Peak is usually the hardest phase to call in real time, because lagging and coincident data can still look strong even as leading indicators start rolling over
Trough has the widest gap between leading data, which turns up first, and lagging data, which is often still weak
Equity markets have historically behaved as a leading indicator themselves, bottoming before GDP growth data confirmed the trough in both 2009 and 2020
Chapters 2 through 5 each build out one part of this picture in depth: rate and credit signals, real-economy recession data, recovery identification, and portfolio positioning
